sounds.intro: No one recorded Old Norse as sound, but the Icelandic First Grammatical Treatise (mid-1100s), rhyme and alliteration in poetry, runic spellings and the modern Nordic languages let scholars reconstruct it closely. This guide follows the reconstructed Icelandic of the 1200s used in Gordon's and Byock's textbooks. It differs a good deal from modern Icelandic, which many Icelanders use when they read the sagas aloud.

tips.p: Stress always falls on the first syllable: Óðinn, víkingr, jǫtunn. Compounds such as Miðgarðr take a lighter second stress on the second part.
Vowel length and consonant length both change meaning: far 'ship' and fár 'few'; sin 'sinew' and sinn 'his own'. Poets counted long and short syllables, so length matters for metre too.
In maðr, sonr and hestr the r follows the consonant with no vowel between. Around 1300 Icelanders began to insert u, which gives modern maður, sonur, hestur.

The First Grammatical Treatise describes Icelandic vowels precisely, including length and nasal vowels, and rhymes in skaldic verse confirm many details. The exact quality of v, au and runic ʀ is less certain.
Many Icelanders read the sagas in modern pronunciation: á as [au], é as [jɛ], æ as [ai], ll as [tl], hv as [kv]. Both ways are legitimate. This course spells and describes the medieval forms.

grammar.title: The article on the end
grammar.note: -inn for masculine, -in for feminine, -it for neuter. A final -a drops, and so does the i after a vowel.

grammar.title: Subject and object
grammar.note: The object (accusative) of a masculine in -r drops the -r, a weak feminine changes -a to -u, and a neuter does not change. Names follow suit: Þórr, Þór; Óðinn, Óðin.

grammar.title: Strong verbs, present: fara, koma, sjá
grammar.note: Many strong verbs change their vowel in the singular. 'You' and 'he' share a form.
head: fara 'go'
koma 'come'
sjá 'see'

grammar.title: hafa 'have' and gefa 'give', present
grammar.note: Both take an object in the accusative. hafa is weak but irregular in the present.
head: hafa
gefa

grammar.title: Strong verbs, past: fara, gefa, vera
grammar.note: No ending for 'I' and 'he', -t for 'you'. The plural often has a different vowel.
head: fara 'go'
gefa 'give'
vera 'be'

grammar.title: Weak verbs: kalla 'call'
grammar.note: The past adds -að- (or -ð-, -d-, -t- in other verbs: hafði, sigldi). A u in the ending turns a into ǫ.

grammar.title: Strong neuter and feminine: skip 'ship', hlíð 'slope'
grammar.note: Neuters are the same in nominative and accusative, singular and plural. Strong feminines often end the genitive in -ar.

grammar.title: Weak nouns: bogi 'bow', kona 'woman'
grammar.note: Weak nouns end in a vowel and have one form for all the other singular cases. The genitive plural of kona is irregular.

grammar.title: Personal pronouns
grammar.note: The genitive serves after some prepositions (til mín) and as 'his', 'her', 'their' (hans, hennar, þeira). The reflexive sik points back to the subject.

grammar.note: þinn 'your' and sinn 'his, her, their own' decline the same way. The possessive usually follows its noun: faðir minn.
